pages.text: Millions of years ago, a special path of land formed. It connected Eurasia and Afro-Arabia. This land bridge changed the history of animals on Earth. It let many creatures walk between these big land areas for the very first time in a very long while.
pages.caption: Apterodon langebadreae, an apterodontine hyaenodont

evidence.articleCaption: Apterodon langebadreae, an apterodontine hyaenodont

pages.text: Before this land bridge appeared, Africa was cut off from other places. It spent a very long time as a large island continent. Because of this, unique animals lived there. These included early proboscideans, which are related to modern elephants.
pages.caption: Barytherium, a basal proboscidean

evidence.articleCaption: Barytherium, a basal proboscidean

pages.text: Then, during the Early Miocene, tectonic plates crashed together. They created a new land connection between the two massive regions. This big event is known as the Great Old World Biotic Interchange. Animals started to cross over in both directions.
pages.caption: Arsinoitherium, a derived embrithopod

evidence.articleCaption: Arsinoitherium, a derived embrithopod

pages.text: With the new bridge open, animals began to travel far. Elephant ancestors called gomphotheres walked out of Africa and into Eurasia. At the same time, new predators and ungulates crossed over from Eurasia to make their homes in Afro-Arabia.
pages.caption: Pterodon dasyuroides, a hyainailourine

evidence.articleCaption: Pterodon dasyuroides, a hyainailourine

pages.text: Not all animals could cross the bridge easily. Open habitats and environmental changes created strong barriers for certain species. Even so, this major event forever changed the wildlife found across the continents.

The Gomphotherium land bridge was a significant terrestrial connection linking Eurasia to Afro-Arabia. While originally dated between approximately 19 and 15 million years ago during the Early Miocene, more recent analysis suggests it may have formed slightly earlier, around 20 million years ago. This formation ended a long period of biogeographic isolation for Africa.

evidence.articleCaption: Apterodon langebadreae, an apterodontine hyaenodont

pages.text: For much of the Cenozoic, Africa remained an island continent. Its endemic mammalian fauna largely consisted of groups like Afrotheria, including early proboscideans which first evolved in Africa around 60 million years ago. Over time, some of these early elephant relatives grew significantly in size and developed diverse forms.
pages.caption: Barytherium, a basal proboscidean

evidence.articleCaption: Barytherium, a basal proboscidean

pages.text: The collision of the Afro-Arabian and Eurasian tectonic plates created a terrestrial isthmus that bridged the two landmasses. This monumental event triggered the Great Old World Biotic Interchange, also referred to as the Proboscidean Datum Event. Fauna from Eurasia migrated into Afro-Arabia, and vice versa.
pages.caption: Arsinoitherium, a derived embrithopod

evidence.articleCaption: Arsinoitherium, a derived embrithopod

pages.text: The newly formed bridge enabled elephantine gomphotheres and other proboscideans to migrate out of Africa and into Eurasia. Simultaneously, Eurasian ungulates and various mammalian predators were able to disperse into Africa. This exchange transformed the ecological makeup of both regions.
pages.caption: Pterodon dasyuroides, a hyainailourine

evidence.articleCaption: Pterodon dasyuroides, a hyainailourine

pages.text: However, the faunal exchange displayed notable asymmetry. Environmental shifts, such as the spread of open and arid habitats, created strong barriers that limited certain migrations. Furthermore, differences in diversity and locomotor abilities influenced how various native and immigrant species adapted to the changing landscapes.

C1-C2.headline: The Great Old World Biotic Interchange

pages.text: The Gomphotherium land bridge constituted a pivotal tectonic connection uniting Eurasia with Afro-Arabia during the Burdigalian stage of the Early Miocene. Although classical estimates place its emergence between 19 and 15 million years ago, subsequent analyses propose an earlier formation around 20 million years ago. This geological milestone terminated Africa's 75-million-year biogeographic isolation.
pages.caption: Apterodon langebadreae, an apterodontine hyaenodont

evidence.articleCaption: Apterodon langebadreae, an apterodontine hyaenodont

pages.text: Functioning largely as an insular landmass throughout the Cretaceous and much of the Cenozoic, Africa fostered an endemic mammalian assemblage dominated by afrotherians, including primitive proboscideans originating in the Paleocene. Subsequent evolutionary diversification yielded increasingly large taxa, transitioning from small forms to substantial semi-aquatic and terrestrial herbivores by the Eocene and Oligocene epochs.

pages.text: The mid-Burdigalian tectonic collision between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia generated a terrestrial isthmus that facilitated bidirectional faunal migration. This extensive biotic transference is formally recognized as the Proboscidean Datum Event or the Great Old World Biotic Interchange. It allowed taxa previously separated by the open Tethyan seaway to traverse continental boundaries.

pages.text: Consequent to this structural linkage, gomphotheres and assorted proboscideans successfully emigrated from Africa into Eurasia. Reciprocally, Eurasian carnivorans and ungulates colonized Afro-Arabia. These dispersive pulses restructured regional predator guilds, instigating direct pressures on native apex predators such as hyaenodonts.

Disparities in ancestral taxonomic diversity, combined with progressive aridification and the expansion of open savanna and steppe environments, constrained dispersals. These shifting ecological barriers ultimately precipitated the localized decline of lineages poorly adapted to open, seasonal habitats.

pages.text: Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership and profit. It includes private property, competitive markets, and wage labor. Modern capitalism evolved from agrarianism in England and mercantilist practices in Europe between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries. Its exact emergence remains a subject of extensive research and debate.

pages.text: Some historians argue that the roots of modern capitalism begin in the crisis of the Late Middle Ages. This period involved conflicts between the land-owning aristocracy and agricultural serfs. Manorial arrangements stopped early capitalist development because serfs had forced obligations to lords who relied on military power.

pages.text: During the fourteenth century, demographic crises upset this feudal arrangement. Agricultural productivity reached limits, bad weather caused a famine, and the Black Death caused a population crash. In England, many serfs rebelled, moved to towns, bought land, or entered into rental contracts.

pages.text: By the sixteenth century, England was a centralized state with a large internal market centered on London. The old manorial system broke down as land concentrated into larger estates. Landlords and tenants faced new pressures to increase agricultural productivity for profit within a competitive labor market.

pages.text: Trade has existed for thousands of years, but early trade was not capitalism. Capitalism took shape in Europe during the late Middle Ages and Renaissance. Later, the eighteenth-century Industrial Revolution cemented capitalism as the primary method of production through factories and the use of steam power.

In the twentieth century, capitalism faced major challenges including the Russian Revolution and the Great Depression. Different responses included state capitalism, communism, and socialism. Later, post-war economic recovery brought renewed growth, and states began playing a prominent role to regulate the capitalist system.

Capitalism is an economic system defined by the private ownership of the means of production used to obtain profit. Key features include private property, capital accumulation, competitive markets, and wage labor. Modern capitalism gradually evolved from English agrarianism and European mercantilism between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, becoming the primary mode of production during the Industrial Revolution.

pages.text: While long-distance trade has existed since ancient times, historians debate the exact origins of capitalism. Some trace its roots to the crisis of the Late Middle Ages, highlighting conflicts between the land-owning aristocracy and agricultural producers. Traditional manorial systems relied on force and military obligations, which inhibited the development of flexible economic markets.

pages.text: A severe demographic crisis in the fourteenth century disrupted feudal structures. Agricultural productivity limits, the Great Famine, and the devastating Black Death combined to cause a major population crash. In response to lords demanding higher tribute, English serfs rebelled, migrated to towns, purchased land, or secured favorable rental contracts.

pages.text: By the sixteenth century, England developed a centralized state with London acting as a massive internal market. The breakdown of the manorial system concentrated land into fewer large estates. Economic incentives shifted as land rents became subject to market forces rather than custom, pushing both landlords and tenants to increase agricultural productivity.

pages.text: During the early modern period, mercantilist practices spread across Europe, supported by state controls, monopolies, and chartered trading companies like the Muscovy Company. Eventually, eighteenth-century theorists like Adam Smith challenged mercantilism. Concurrently, the Industrial Revolution introduced machine production, steam power, and advanced banking systems.

The twentieth century tested capitalist economies through the 1917 Russian Revolution and the Great Depression, which sparked alternative systems like fascism and communism. Following the Second World War, rapid economic growth and increased state regulation stabilized capitalism. Today, ongoing debates examine whether globalization has transformed capitalism into a true world system.

Capitalism constitutes an economic system grounded in private ownership of production means directed toward profit generation. Its foundational components encompass commodification, wage labor, competitive markets, and capital accumulation. Historical scholarship extensively debates its emergence from sixteenth to eighteenth-century European mercantilism and English agrarianism, solidified subsequently by the Industrial Revolution.

Certain historians locate its genesis in the crisis of the Late Middle Ages, emphasizing structural conflicts between aristocratic landowners and serfs. Traditional manorial arrangements relied on coercive extractions, which structurally impeded market-driven economic development.

pages.text: Fourteenth-century demographic shocks severely destabilized feudal relations. The convergence of agricultural stagnation, the Great Famine, and the mortality rates of the Black Death precipitated a profound population contraction. Consequently, English serfs utilized various strategies of resistance, including rebellion, urban migration, land acquisition, and advantageous rental agreements.

pages.text: Sixteenth-century England exhibited advanced state centralization, wherein London functioned as an integrated national market. The dissolution of traditional manorial structures facilitated land consolidation among fewer landlords. Market forces progressively superseded custom in determining land rents, thereby compelling landlords and tenants alike to elevate productivity within competitive labor markets.

pages.text: Early modern mercantilism utilized state monopolies, subsidies, and chartered entities such as the Muscovy Company to regulate commerce. This framework was later contested by classical economic theorists like Adam Smith, aligning with the onset of the Industrial Revolution. The ensuing industrial expansion catalyzed sophisticated credit systems, including centralized banking clearing houses.

Key features include private property, capital accumulation, competitive markets, and wage labor. Modern capitalism gradually evolved from English agrarianism and European mercantilism between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, becoming the primary mode of production during the Industrial Revolution.

pages.text: Visual costumbrismo developed among painters in Spain. Madrid and Andalusia were the two great centers. Andalusian paintings were romantic and folkloric for foreign buyers. The painters in Madrid were more critical and focused on lower-class life. Other artists brought these traditions to Mexico and Bolivia.

Costumbrismo is the literary or pictorial interpretation of local everyday life, mannerisms, and customs, particularly within the Hispanic scene during the nineteenth century. Related to both artistic realism and Romanticism, it focuses on the precise representation of particular times and places. While often satiric or moralizing, it generally avoids deep societal analysis.

pages.text: The history of technology is the story of human invention. People create new tools using new knowledge. Technology includes simple stone tools and complex engineering. Technical history is connected to science and economics. Technological change affects our culture and traditions every day.

pages.text: During the Stone Age, humans lived with limited tools and few permanent settlements. The first tools were for survival, hunting, and food preparation. Major developments included stone weapons, fire, and clothing. Later, people found native copper before they knew how to smelt metal ores.

pages.text: Ancient civilizations built great structures. The Egyptians used simple machines like ramps and levers to build massive pyramids. The Indus Valley Civilization used early city planning and plumbing. China created many early developments, including paper, the compass, and gunpowder for various uses.

pages.text: During the medieval period, water and wind power became very important for milling grain and other tasks. pages.text: The Industrial Revolution was driven by cheap energy from coal in Britain. It brought major developments in textile machinery, mining, metallurgy, and transport. Later, the Second Industrial Revolution brought rapid innovation in chemical, electrical, petroleum, and steel technologies across Europe until World War I.

The history of technology traces how humans have invented tools and techniques from simple stone implements to complex genetic engineering. Because much of technology represents applied science and resource utilization, technical history connects closely with both scientific and economic development. These changes significantly influence cultural traditions and serve as major forces for economic growth and political power.
